cards.explanation: The answer is that Mordecai tears his clothes and puts on sackcloth. Mordecai, who raised Esther (Esther 2:7), tears his clothes and puts on sackcloth and ashes (Esther 4:1). In this chapter, that's what mourning looks like (Esther 4:3). He doesn't keep it quiet, either, because he goes out into the middle of the city, wailing loudly and bitterly. His clothes and his voice say the same thing, friends.

The answer is that the law kept anyone in sackcloth out. Esther 4:2 says Mordecai went only as far as the king's gate, "…because the law prohibited anyone wearing sackcloth from entering that gate." So he walks right up to the edge and stops. The sackcloth that shows his grief is the same thing that keeps him out. That's a rough spot to be stuck in, friends.

The word is "fast." Esther 4:3 says that in every province to which the king's command and edict came, there was great mourning among the Jews. "They fasted, wept, and lamented, and many lay in sackcloth and ashes." Fasting means going without food, and it's part of how they mourn. News about the decree travels far, and so does the grief. It's a sad picture, friends, and I think we should let it be sad.

The answer is clothes to wear instead of sackcloth. Esther 4:4 says that when her maidens and eunuchs told her about Mordecai, the queen was overcome with distress. She sent clothes for Mordecai to wear instead of his sackcloth. Her first move is to get him something else to wear, and that's a caring thing to do, friends. I think she wanted to help however she could.
The answer is False. Esther sent clothes for Mordecai to wear instead of his sackcloth, but he would not accept them (Esther 4:4). Mordecai turns the clothes down. Her gift gets a no.

The answer is True. Esther summoned Hathach, one of the king's eunuchs appointed to her. She sent him to Mordecai "…to learn what was troubling him and why." (Esther 4:5). So she sends someone to go find out what's troubling him. Hathach is about to get a lot of steps in.

The answer is how much money Haman promised to pay. Esther 4:7 says Mordecai told Hathach all that had happened, including "…the exact amount of money that Haman had promised to pay into the royal treasury in order to destroy the Jews." Haman is the king's top official (Esther 3:1). Mordecai passes along the exact figure. That's a very specific detail, friends.

The answer is a copy of the written decree. Esther 4:8 says Mordecai gave Hathach "…a copy of the written decree issued in Susa for the destruction of the Jews…" to show and explain to Esther. So she gets to see the decree itself, not just hear about it. Hathach carries it to her and explains it. That's a lot to put in someone's hands, friends.

The answer is True. Esther 4:8 says Mordecai urged her "…to approach the king, implore his favor, and plead before him for her people." He gives her the decree and the request together. It's a big ask, and he doesn't water it down.

The answer is that they are put to death. Esther says one law applies to every man or woman who approaches the king in the inner court without being summoned: "…that he be put to death." (Esther 4:11). Only if the king extends the gold scepter may that person live. So walking in uninvited is a very risky move. That's the whole problem, friends.

The answer is that the palace will keep her safe. Mordecai says, "Do not imagine that because you are in the king’s palace you alone will escape the fate of all the Jews." (Esther 4:13) Esther is living inside the palace. Mordecai tells her not to imagine that being there means she alone will escape. That's a tough thing to hear, friends.

The answer is False. Mordecai says, "…relief and deliverance for the Jews will arise from another place, but you and your father’s house will perish." (Esther 4:14) He doesn't say there's no other hope. His warning is about what silence would cost Esther and her family.

The word is "perish." Mordecai says that if she remains silent, relief for the Jews will arise from another place, "…but you and your father’s house will perish." (Esther 4:14) Perish is a strong word. I think Mordecai wants her to hear how serious this is. There's no sprinkles on that sentence, friends.

The answer is that maybe she became queen for this very moment. Mordecai asks, "And who knows if perhaps you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" (Esther 4:14) He asks it as a question and leaves it open. He's inviting Esther to think about why she is where she is. It's a question that makes you sit up, friends.

The answer is to fast for her for three days. Esther says to assemble all the Jews who can be found in Susa and "…fast for me. Do not eat or drink for three days, night or day…" (Esther 4:16) That's no food and no drink for three days. It's a serious request, friends. She's asking the people to stand with her.

The word is "maidens." Esther says, "…I and my maidens will fast as you do." (Esther 4:16) She isn't asking the people to do something she won't do herself. Her maidens are in it with her. That's a queen who fasts right alongside everybody.

The answer is True. Esther says, "After that, I will go to the king, even though it is against the law." (Esther 4:16) First comes the fast, and after that she says she will go. She knows what the law says about going uninvited (Esther 4:11), and she says it anyway.

The answer is True. Esther 4:17 says, "So Mordecai went and did all that Esther had instructed him." Earlier it was Mordecai giving the instructions. Now Esther gives them, and he follows them. The story isn't over, friends.
